title: Arrays & Hashing
html:
Arrays & Hashing

Arrays and hash tables are the two structures most problems reduce to. Knowing what each costs, and where the cost stops being what you assumed, is most of the value.

Arrays

A contiguous block of memory. That one fact explains every property:

Operation Cost Why
Index read/write O(1) address = base + index x element size
Append, amortised O(1) doubling spreads growth cost over many appends
Insert or remove at front or middle O(n) everything after it shifts
Search, unsorted O(n) no structure to exploit
Search, sorted O(log n) binary search

Contiguity also makes arrays fast in ways the table does not show. A cache line is typically 64 bytes, so walking an array pulls the next several elements in for free, while a linked structure pays a cache miss per node. This is why an O(n) array scan often beats an O(log n) tree walk at small sizes: asymptotics describe growth, not speed.

Hash tables

Average O(1) insert, lookup and delete, by turning a key into a bucket index.

What that average hides:

  • Collisions. Two keys in one bucket, resolved by chaining or by probing for the next free slot. Worst case degrades to O(n).
  • Resizing. Crossing the load factor rebuilds the table, so one insert in many is O(n).
  • Hash quality. A poor hash concentrates keys into few buckets. This is a real attack: deliberately colliding keys turn an O(1) endpoint into O(n) per request.
  • Ordering. There is none. Anything depending on order needs a structure that promises it.

Equality is the part that goes wrong

A hash table needs two things from a key - a hash code and equality - and they must agree. Two equal keys must hash identically, or a lookup fails to find what was inserted.

The failure is silent. A mutable key whose hash changes after insertion is lost inside its own table: the entry is there, the bucket it now hashes to is empty, and nothing reports a problem. Use immutable keys.

Patterns worth recognising

Seen-set. One pass, remembering what has appeared. Turns "is there a duplicate" and "does a complement exist" from O(n squared) into O(n).

Frequency map. Count, then reason over counts. Anagrams, most-common-k, "does one string cover another".

Grouping by a canonical key. Map equivalent items to the same key - sorted letters, a normalised shape - then group. The skill is choosing a key where equality means what you intend.

Prefix sums. Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction. Combined with a map of seen prefix values it answers "how many subarrays sum to k" in a single pass. Worth internalising: a range question becomes a difference of two prefixes.

Index as storage. When values are bounded and near their index range, the array itself can record presence - negate, or swap into place - giving O(1) extra space where a set costs O(n).

Common mistakes

  • Removing from a list while iterating it. Iterate backwards, or build a new one.
  • Assuming O(1) hashing for long string keys; hashing costs O(key length).
  • Using an unordered set and then relying on the output order.
  • Writing a nested loop where a seen-set would do. O(n squared) is fine at n=100 and fatal at n=100,000.
